thing: Thalidomide (Kevadon), a sedative marketed as safe for morning sickness
claim: The safety data were inadequate and the drug might have toxic effects not yet seen; it should not be approved without well-designed studies.
what_happened: In November 1961 Lenz and McBride linked thalidomide to severe birth defects; Richardson-Merrell withdrew its US application in March 1962 and the drug was pulled worldwide.
dismissed_by: Richardson-Merrell, whose representative complained to her superiors she was unreasonable and nit-picking; the drug was already approved in Canada and 20+ countries
cost_of_error: More than 10,000 (possibly up to 20,000) babies born with deformities in 46 countries, ~40% died near birth; the US was largely spared (17 confirmed malformed births from 'experimental' tablets)
lesson: When approval elsewhere is offered as the evidence of safety, ask for the underlying studies; testimonials and momentum are not data.

quotes.text: The clinical reports were more on the nature of testimonials," says Kelsey, "rather than the results of well-designed, well-executed studies.
quotes.speaker: Frances Oldham Kelsey
quotes.publication: FDA Consumer (Linda Bren, 'Frances Oldham Kelsey: FDA Medical Reviewer Leaves Her Mark on History')

quotes.text: We felt that there might be conditions, illnesses, or other drugs that might change the absorption, and toxic effects might appear.
quotes.speaker: Frances Oldham Kelsey

thing: Vioxx (rofecoxib), Merck's COX-2 painkiller marketed as gentler on the stomach
claim: Vioxx raises the risk of heart attack and stroke, and Merck's 'naproxen is protective' explanation for the VIGOR signal is implausible.
what_happened: Merck withdrew Vioxx in September 2004 after its APPROVe trial confirmed elevated cardiovascular risk; FDA epidemiologist David Graham told the Senate it may be the greatest drug safety catastrophe in US history.
dismissed_by: Merck, which attributed the VIGOR heart-attack gap to a protective effect of naproxen and kept marketing; FDA superiors who pressured Graham over his findings
cost_of_error: Graham estimated 88,000-139,000 excess US heart attacks, 30-40% probably fatal; Merck paid a $4.85B mass-tort settlement (2007) plus a $321.6M criminal fine; ~$2.5B/yr in sales before withdrawal
lesson: When the sponsor explains away an adverse signal with a convenient secondary theory, demand the trial that would falsify it before scaling exposure.

quotes.text: Your promotional campaign discounts the fact that in the VIGOR study, patients on Vioxx were observed to have a four- to five-fold increase in myocardial infarctions (MIs) compared to patients on the comparator nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), Naprosyn (naproxen).
quotes.speaker: US FDA warning letter to Merck CEO

quotes.text: Today, in 2004, you, we, are faced with what may be the single greatest drug safety catastrophe in the history of this country or the history of the world.
quotes.speaker: David J. Graham, FDA Office of Drug Safety
quotes.publication: Testimony to the US Senate Finance Committee, November 18, 2004

quotes.text: I would argue that the FDA, as currently configured, is incapable of protecting America against another Vioxx. We are virtually defenseless.
quotes.speaker: David J. Graham, FDA Office of Drug Safety
quotes.publication: Testimony to the US Senate Finance Committee, November 18, 2004

thing: OxyContin, Purdue Pharma's extended-release oxycodone marketed for chronic non-cancer pain
claim: OxyContin is being widely abused and is addictive, contrary to Purdue's claim that addiction risk was 'less than one percent'.
what_happened: Purdue pleaded guilty in 2007 to misleading the public about OxyContin's addiction risk, pleaded guilty again to federal felonies in 2020, went bankrupt, and its marketing is widely tied to the first wave of the US opioid epidemic.
dismissed_by: Purdue Pharma, which trained reps to tell doctors addiction risk was 'less than one percent' and offered 'cosmetic and symbolic steps'; much of the pain-medicine establishment that promoted opioids for chronic pain
cost_of_error: ~806,000 US opioid overdose deaths 1999-2023 (prescription and illicit, per CDC); $600M 2007 plea plus $34.5M executive fines; ~$8B 2020 federal settlement; Sacklers ~$6B bankruptcy contribution
lesson: When a habit-forming product's growth depends on a precise low-risk number, ask where the number came from; the claim of safety is the part that sells.

quotes.text: Purdue Pharma has a moral, if not legal obligation to take effective steps and address addiction and abuse even as it works to reformulate the drug.
quotes.speaker: Richard Blumenthal, Connecticut Attorney General

thing: Radium tonics such as Radithor (radium dissolved in water), sold as an energising 'mild radium therapy'
claim: Ingested radium lodges in bone and kills, as pathologist Harrison Martland showed in the New Jersey radium dial painters; radium 'cures' are not harmless.
what_happened: Steel magnate Eben Byers drank ~1,400 bottles of Radithor and died of radium poisoning in 1932 with much of his jaw removed; the FTC ordered Bailey to stop calling Radithor harmless, and the publicity ended the radium-tonic era.
dismissed_by: Manufacturer William J. A. Bailey (who paid doctors a kickback per dose) and prescribing physician C.C. Moyar, who denied radium killed Byers and said he drank it himself
cost_of_error: Byers's death plus an unknown toll among the buyers of 400,000+ bottles of Radithor; the related radium dial painters were among those Martland documented dying of radium poisoning
lesson: A product that borrows the prestige of a frontier science while skipping its safety literature is selling the prestige; check what the field's own pathologists already know.

quotes.text: his whole upper jaw, excepting two front teeth, and most of his lower jaw had been removed. All the remaining bone tissue of his body was slowly disintegrating, and holes were actually forming in his skull.
quotes.speaker: Robert Winn, Federal Trade Commission attorney
quotes.publication: FTC interview report, quoted by ORAU Museum of Radiation and Radioactivity

quotes.text: cease and desist from various representations theretofore made by them as to the therapeutic value of Radithor and from representing that the product Radithor is harmless.
quotes.speaker: Federal Trade Commission order against Bailey Radium Laboratories
quotes.publication: FTC order, December 19, 1931, quoted by ORAU

thing: Diethylstilbestrol (DES), a synthetic estrogen prescribed to pregnant women to prevent miscarriage
claim: A double-blind trial (Dieckmann, University of Chicago) showed DES gives no benefit in pregnancy, so exposing mothers and fetuses to it is unjustified.
what_happened: DES kept being prescribed through the 1960s; in 1971 Herbst linked in-utero exposure to vaginal clear-cell adenocarcinoma and the FDA advised against use in pregnancy, with later harms including infertility and pregnancy complications in exposed daughters.
dismissed_by: Manufacturers who aggressively marketed DES (sales peaked in 1953) and obstetricians who kept prescribing it for nearly two decades despite the null trial
cost_of_error: Up to ~2 million US mothers and fetuses exposed 1940-1971; DES daughters carry ~40x the risk of clear-cell adenocarcinoma (~1 in 1,000) and elevated infertility (33% vs 15%) and premature delivery (53% vs 18%) per NCI
lesson: A treatment shown not to work is never neutral: if the null result is ignored, every later unknown harm is pure loss, so stop on the efficacy evidence rather than waiting for the safety evidence.

claim: Cigarette smoking is an important cause of lung cancer (Doll & Hill, BMJ 1950; Wynder & Graham, JAMA 1950).
what_happened: The British Doctors Study confirmed the link by 1956, the US Surgeon General's 1964 report declared smoking a health hazard warranting action, and internal documents later showed the industry knew while manufacturing doubt.
dismissed_by: The tobacco industry's 1954 'Frank Statement' (no proof smoking causes cancer; statistics could apply to many aspects of modern life) and its Tobacco Industry Research Committee
cost_of_error: Smoking and secondhand smoke cause 480,000+ US deaths a year and 16M+ Americans live with smoking-caused disease (CDC); 1998 Master Settlement Agreement committed at least $206B over 25 years
lesson: When an industry's answer to an epidemiological signal is a research committee rather than a trial, treat 'more research is needed' as a business strategy, not a scientific position.

quotes.text: cigarette smoking is a health hazard of sufficient importance in the United States to warrant appropriate remedial action,
quotes.speaker: US Surgeon General's Advisory Committee (Luther Terry)
quotes.publication: Smoking and Health, quoted by NLM Profiles in Science

quotes.text: That there was no proof that cigarette smoking is one of the causes.
quotes.speaker: Tobacco Industry Research Committee, 'A Frank Statement to Cigarette Smokers' (summarised claim)

thing: Artificial trans fats from partially hydrogenated oils (shortening, margarine, processed foods)
claim: Artificial trans fats accumulate in human tissue and contribute to heart disease (Fred Kummerow, Science 1957, then a 50-year campaign).
what_happened: Nurses' Health Study and later work confirmed the trans fat-heart disease link; labeling was required from 2006 and in 2015 the FDA ruled PHOs no longer Generally Recognized as Safe, banning them from 2018 (final compliance 2021).
dismissed_by: The food industry, which met his 1957 paper with scorn and kept PHOs as a cheap shelf-stable fat; the FDA, which sat on his 2009 ban petition until he sued in 2013
cost_of_error: Decades of avoidable heart disease; FDA says removing PHOs is preventing thousands of heart attacks and deaths each year (other estimates run to tens of thousands)
lesson: An ingredient grandfathered as 'generally recognized as safe' is safe by default, not by evidence, so a lone credible dissenter on a cheap, ubiquitous input deserves a test, not a shrug.

quotes.text: Artificial trans fat is a poisonous and deleterious substance, and the FDA has acknowledged the danger.
quotes.speaker: Fred Kummerow (FDA petition/lawsuit)

quotes.text: In 2015, the FDA took the significant step of determining that PHOs, then the major source of artificial trans fat in the food supply, are no longer “Generally Recognized as Safe,” or GRAS.
quotes.speaker: US Food and Drug Administration

claim: Fenfluramine-class drugs cause primary pulmonary hypertension far more often than the label admits, a risk not warranted by their minimal weight loss; Redux needed a black-box warning.
what_happened: After a 1997 Mayo Clinic NEJM report of valvular heart disease and ~30% abnormal echocardiograms in long-term users, the FDA requested withdrawal of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine in September 1997.
dismissed_by: FDA management, which had another official sign Redux's 1996 approval with no black-box warning after Lutwak refused; Wyeth, which listed 4 pulmonary hypertension cases on the label when 41 had been observed
cost_of_error: Valve damage in a large share of long-term users (~30% abnormal echocardiograms), fatal pulmonary hypertension cases, 50,000+ product-liability suits and Wyeth reserves of $21.1B
lesson: For a mass-market lifestyle drug, a rare-but-irreversible harm has to be weighed against modest benefit times millions of users; a reviewer who says the counts look higher than the label deserves the black box.

quotes.text: When I started looking at the actual reports, it didn't seem that rare. Taking that in consideration of the minimal weight loss seen with it, it seemed to me this was a risk that was not warranted.
quotes.speaker: Leo Lutwak, FDA medical officer

claim: The Dalkon Shield's multifilament tail string wicks bacteria into the uterus and needs fixing before sale.
what_happened: Septic abortions, pelvic infections, infertility and deaths followed; FDA pressed Robins to suspend US sales in 1974, more than 327,000 claims were filed and Robins went bankrupt in 1985.
dismissed_by: A.H. Robins management, which rejected heat-sealing the string as too costly, denied a link to septicemia, kept selling abroad until 1980 and later ordered wicking documents destroyed
cost_of_error: ~2.2M US users at peak; 327,000+ lawsuits and claims; $2.5B claimant trust in bankruptcy; no IUDs on the US market 1983-1988, setting back a useful contraceptive class for years
lesson: When your own quality-control staff flag a cheap-to-fix defect and the fix is rejected on cost, the liability has already been booked, just not yet billed.

quotes.text: the string or tail situation needs a careful review since the present tail is reported (by a co-inventor) to have a wicking tendency.
quotes.speaker: Robert Nickless, A.H. Robins product management coordinator (internal memo)
quotes.publication: Los Angeles Times, 'The Right Question: One Man's Effort to Tell Dalkon Story' (1985)

quotes.text: Robins quality control supervisor Wayne Crowder warned that his tests indicated the string would wick bacteria.
quotes.speaker: Los Angeles Times (Barry Siegel), describing Crowder's 1971 memo

thing: Theranos finger-prick blood testing (Edison device) promising hundreds of tests from a few drops
claim: Theranos's technology has no peer-reviewed validation, and its claims are likely exaggerated or false ('stealth research').
what_happened: WSJ's Carreyrou reported in October 2015 that most tests ran on conventional analyzers; CMS sanctions followed, the SEC charged an 'elaborate, years-long fraud' in 2018, the company dissolved in 2018 and Holmes and Balwani were convicted in 2022.
dismissed_by: Theranos (called the reporting 'factually and scientifically erroneous' and sent lawyers after sources), its celebrity board, Walgreens, and investors who skipped diligence
cost_of_error: $700M+ raised at a ~$9B peak valuation wiped out; patients received inaccurate results (Arizona alone: $4.65M refunds to every tested resident); Holmes sentenced to 11 years 3 months
lesson: A health or deep-tech company that is famous in the business press but absent from the peer-reviewed literature is asking you to substitute its board's reputation for data.

quotes.text: Information about Theranos, a privately held biotechnology company that has developed novel approaches for laboratory diagnostic testing, has appeared in The Wall Street Journal, Business Insider, San Francisco Business Times, Fortune, Forbes, Medscape, and Silicon Valley Business Journal—but not in the peer-reviewed biomedical literature.
quotes.speaker: John P. A. Ioannidis
quotes.publication: JAMA, 'Stealth Research: Is Biomedical Innovation Happening Outside the Peer-Reviewed Literature?'

quotes.text: raising more than $700 million from investors through an elaborate, years-long fraud in which they exaggerated or made false statements about the company’s technology, business, and financial performance.
quotes.speaker: US Securities and Exchange Commission

thing: Juul high-nicotine-salt pod e-cigarette with flavored pods and social-media marketing
claim: Juul-style e-cigarettes are hooking teenagers on nicotine at epidemic scale and reversing decades of decline in youth nicotine use.
what_happened: Youth vaping did surge (12th-grade nicotine vaping roughly doubled 11% to 21% in 2017-18), Juul paid $3B+ in youth-marketing settlements and its valuation fell from $38B to ~$450M; but youth cigarette smoking kept falling, high-school e-cig use fell to 7.1% by 2025, and long-term harm versus adult cessation benefit is still contested.
dismissed_by: Juul Labs, which said it was for adult smokers while buying ads on Nick Jr., Seventeen and student game sites; Altria, which invested $12.8B in December 2018
cost_of_error: Millions of teens exposed to high-dose nicotine; Juul settlements of at least $3B including $462M to six states and DC (2023); Altria wrote its $12.8B stake down to ~3.5% of value
lesson: Youth-uptake fears about a new habit-forming product tend to be right about the first-order surge and wrong about the long-run apocalypse; plan for the regulatory and legal backlash, not for the predicted generation lost.

quotes.text: We didn’t predict what I now believe is an epidemic of e-cigarette use among teenagers. Today we can see that this epidemic of addiction was emerging when we first announced our plan last summer.
quotes.speaker: Scott Gottlieb, FDA Commissioner

thing: Long-term menopausal hormone replacement therapy (estrogen plus progestin) promoted to prevent heart disease and aging
claim: Combined HRT taken for chronic-disease prevention raises breast cancer, heart disease, stroke and clot risk, so risks exceed benefits (Women's Health Initiative).
what_happened: WHI's combined-hormone arm was stopped in 2002 and HRT use collapsed; later reanalyses found risk depends heavily on age and time since menopause, and in November 2025 the FDA removed cardiovascular, breast cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning, calling earlier readings overstated (itself debated).
dismissed_by: Pre-2002 observational studies and prescribers that treated cardioprotection as established; after 2002, the reverse error, where clinicians generalised older-women risks to younger symptomatic women
cost_of_error: Before 2002, millions of women took HRT for an unproven heart benefit with excess breast cancer, stroke and clot risk; after 2002, a generation of symptomatic women was arguably steered away from a useful treatment for two decades
lesson: A warning can be right for the population studied and wrong when stretched to everyone; ask who was in the trial before letting a headline flip an entire market in either direction.

quotes.text: Overall health risks exceeded benefits from use of combined estrogen plus progestin for an average 5.2-year follow-up among healthy postmenopausal US women.
quotes.speaker: Writing Group for the Women's Health Initiative Investigators (Rossouw et al.)

quotes.text: By removing these boxed warnings, we ensure that women receive accurate information about hormone therapy—free from exaggeration or fear.
quotes.speaker: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., HHS Secretary
quotes.publication: FDA press announcement, labeling changes to menopausal hormone therapy

thing: Avandia (rosiglitazone), GSK's blockbuster type 2 diabetes drug
claim: Rosiglitazone significantly increases the risk of heart attack (Nissen & Wolski meta-analysis, NEJM 2007).
what_happened: FDA added a boxed warning (2007) and restricted access (2011-2013); Europe suspended it in 2010 and the UK, India and New Zealand withdrew it; but a re-adjudicated RECORD trial found no excess cardiovascular risk and the FDA lifted restrictions in 2013, leaving the size of the harm contested.
dismissed_by: GlaxoSmithKline, which a 2010 Senate Finance report said sought to intimidate critical doctors and which later pleaded guilty partly for withholding cardiovascular safety data; a 2007 FDA panel that voted 22-1 to keep it on the market
cost_of_error: FDA's David Graham estimated 83,000 excess heart attacks 1999-2007; sales fell from ~$2.5B (2006) to $9.5M (2012); GSK paid a $3B DOJ settlement (2012) in part for withholding Avandia safety studies; 13,000+ suits by 2010
lesson: A drug approved on a surrogate marker (blood sugar) can win the number and lose the patient; demand outcome data, and expect a meta-analysis warning to be right on direction even when it is wrong on size.

quotes.text: Rosiglitazone was associated with a significant increase in the risk of myocardial infarction and with an increase in the risk of death from cardiovascular causes that had borderline significance.
quotes.speaker: Steven E. Nissen and Kathy Wolski

thing: Rezulin (troglitazone), Warner-Lambert/Parke-Davis fast-tracked type 2 diabetes pill
claim: Rezulin offers little therapeutic advantage over existing diabetes drugs and could harm the liver and the heart; it should not be approved.
what_happened: Approved in January 1997 after the reviewer was removed; Britain pulled it in December 1997 over liver failure, monitoring failed to prevent deaths, and the FDA withdrew it in March 2000.
dismissed_by: Warner-Lambert, which complained about reviewer John Gueriguian's 'intemperate' language; FDA management, which removed him, purged his review, and later threatened other dissenting staff
cost_of_error: 63 liver-failure deaths linked by withdrawal (LA Times later cited 89 reported liver failures incl. 61 deaths in an earlier FDA tally); $2.1B in sales; ~$750M paid to settle ~35,000 claims (2009)
lesson: When a fast-tracked product's main dissenter is removed for tone rather than rebutted on substance, treat the dissent as the most informative signal in the file.

quotes.text: By the fall of 1996, Gueriguian concluded that Rezulin was unfit for approval and warned of its potential to harm both the liver and the heart.
quotes.speaker: David Willman, Los Angeles Times, describing John L. Gueriguian's FDA review
quotes.publication: Los Angeles Times, 'The Rise and Fall of the Killer Drug Rezulin'

quotes.text: Gueriguian “emphasized that [Rezulin] offered very little significant therapeutic advantage” over existing diabetes medications, according to a summary of an FDA staff meeting on Aug. 22, 1996.
quotes.speaker: FDA staff meeting summary (John L. Gueriguian), quoted by the Los Angeles Times

claim: Cosmetic talc, including J&J Baby Powder, can be contaminated with asbestos and may cause cancer (Mount Sinai researchers' 1971 finding of chrysotile in Baby Powder).
what_happened: Reuters (2018) documented internal reports from 1957 into the 2000s finding tremolite or asbestos in some J&J talc; J&J stopped selling talc baby powder in the US in 2020, settled mesothelioma suits, and saw three bankruptcy strategies rejected, but whether cosmetic talc causes ovarian cancer remains scientifically and legally contested.
dismissed_by: Johnson & Johnson, which told the public its research showed no asbestos in its powder and did not tell the FDA about positive 1972-75 lab tests; most internal tests reported none
cost_of_error: Tens of thousands of ovarian-cancer suits; J&J's rejected $10B bankruptcy settlement (2025) and prior mesothelioma settlements; a 2018 St. Louis verdict of $4.69B (later cut to ~$2.1B)
lesson: A contamination warning about a natural raw material is a supply-chain question you can test continuously; if your defence is that most tests come back clean, the minority that do not is what the court will read.

quotes.text: Later that year, another Mount Sinai researcher, mineralogist Arthur Langer, told J&J in a letter that the team had found a “relatively small” amount of chrysotile asbestos in Baby Powder.
quotes.speaker: Reuters (Lisa Girion), describing Arthur Langer's 1971 letter
quotes.publication: Reuters, 'J&J knew for decades that asbestos lurked in its Baby Powder'

quotes.text: Our fifty years of research knowledge in this area indicates that there is no asbestos contained in the powder manufactured by Johnson & Johnson.
quotes.speaker: Johnson & Johnson statement (dismissal)

quotes.text: J&J stopped selling talc-based baby powder in the U.S. in 2020, switching to a cornstarch product.
quotes.speaker: Reuters (Dietrich Knauth)
quotes.publication: Reuters, 'US judge rejects J&J's $10 billion baby powder settlement'
